card.name: Yayue
card.tagline: The formal, ritualized music and dance of the ancient Chinese imperial court.
card.profile: Yayue, or 'elegant music,' served as the formal, ritualized representation of aristocratic power in ancient China. Established in the Western Zhou dynasty, it functioned as a moral and political tool, distinguishing the refined courtly sphere from popular entertainment. Today, it exists as a reconstructed tradition, preserved in Confucian rituals in Taiwan and studied as a historical foundation for East Asian court arts.
card.insight: In 1116, Emperor Huizong gifted 428 instruments and 572 costumes to Korea, effectively creating a time capsule of ancient Chinese melodies that were later lost in their homeland.
card.profile_long:
Yayue, translated as 'elegant music,' represents the formal, ritualized musical and dance tradition of the ancient Chinese imperial court. Its conventions were established during the Western Zhou dynasty, where it functioned alongside law and rites as a primary representation of aristocratic political power. Confucius famously championed yayue, contrasting it with the 'decadent' popular music of the state of Zheng, and positioning it as a tool for moral self-cultivation and stable governance. The tradition is deeply rooted in the Confucian system, serving as the standard for solemn ceremonies in honor of Heaven, Earth, ancestors, and the imperial family.

The performance of yayue is characterized by its rigidity and formality. Historically, the orchestra was divided into two distinct ensembles representing yin and yang: the dengge (terrace ensemble) and the gongxian (courtyard ensemble). The dengge, the smaller of the two, performed on building terraces and focused on strings and winds, while the larger gongxian performed in the courtyard, utilizing a full array of instruments arranged according to the cardinal directions. The music is described as slow, stately, and monophonic, with little rhythmic variety. When performed, the number of dancers was strictly regulated by the social rank of the patron, with the emperor entitled to 64 dancers in eight rows of eight, while lower-ranking officials were permitted fewer.

Dance in yayue is categorized into two primary types: civil and military. In civil dances, performers hold a yue flute in the left hand and a feather plume in the right. In military dances, performers carry a shield in the left hand and a battleaxe in the right. These performances were integral to various courtly activities, including archery contests, hunting expeditions, and celebrations following military campaigns.

The tradition underwent significant transformations throughout Chinese history. While it remained a pillar of the imperial court through the Qing dynasty, the practice largely disappeared from public view following the fall of the empire in 1911 and the subsequent political changes in 1949. Modern reconstruction efforts began in Taiwan in the 1960s and in mainland China in the 1990s. While some scholars debate the authenticity of these modern revivals—citing the use of contemporary instruments and substitutions—others argue that yayue has always been a fluid tradition that evolved across dynasties. Today, yayue is also studied as the ancestor to several East Asian court traditions, including the gagaku of Japan, the aak of Korea, and the nhã nhạc of Vietnam, which preserved elements of the tradition that were lost in China.

card.sacred_note: Yayue is a ritualized tradition used in Confucian ceremonies and temple rites; it is considered a formal representation of aristocratic and moral power.

sections.origins_and_history: Established in the Western Zhou dynasty by the Duke of Zhou under commission from King Wu. It evolved through the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, eventually becoming reserved for Confucian rituals and imperial ceremonies until the end of the Qing dynasty.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances are divided into civil and military types. Civil dancers hold a yue flute and feather plume; military dancers hold a shield and battleaxe. The number of dancers is strictly determined by rank, ranging from 64 dancers for the emperor to smaller groups for officials.
sections.music_and_instruments: Orchestras are divided into dengge (terrace) and gongxian (courtyard) ensembles. Instruments are categorized by eight materials: silk, bamboo, wood, stone, metal, clay, gourd, and hide. The music is monophonic, slow, and stately.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in imperial courtyards and temples. Costumes and dance objects were historically significant enough to be gifted as state treasures between dynasties and nations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Used for ceremonies honoring Heaven, Earth, and ancestors, as well as diplomatic meetings, archery contests, and military victory celebrations.
sections.notable_figures: Duke of Zhou, King Wu of Zhou, Confucius, Emperor Huizong of Song, Zhu Xi, Chen Yang.
sections.lineage: Western Zhou -> Qin -> Han -> Tang -> Song -> Qing -> Modern Reconstruction (Taiwan/China).

claims.text: Yayue was established in the Western Zhou dynasty as a formal representation of aristocratic power.
Confucius considered yayue to be beneficial and essential for self-cultivation.
The orchestra was divided into two ensembles representing yin and yang.
The number of dancers was strictly regulated by the status of the patron.
In 1116, Emperor Huizong gifted 428 instruments and 572 costumes to Korea.
Modern reconstruction of yayue began in Taiwan in the 1960s and in mainland China in the 1990s.
